We have added a note that, given several weeks of prior atmospheric cooling of the snowpack, it is probable
that this melt would simply have been refrozen in the uppermost centimetres below the surface.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
This paper uses a combination of field observations, satellite observations, and simple/conceptual modelling
to address the important topic of meltwater retention in the percolation zone of the Greenland ice sheet –
about which there is some uncertainty. The paper builds on the finding that meltwater retention has led to the
formation of ice slabs at depth the firn pack, and that the presence of these slabs disrupts the normal process of
meltwater percolation and redistribution.
The paper is quite challenging to comprehend as it contains several elements of work that are not easily linked
and are each quite obscure. Despite several attempts to read and review, I could not form a clear narrative
from the study and, more importantly, I was not persuaded by the arguments presented. Either the narrative
needs to be strengthened, or the arguments need to be made more compelling with further work.
Major
I have identified five major concerns that I hope will act as a guide for the authors to reformulate their paper.
1. Loose language. There is lots of loose language and (for me) too much hyperbole in this paper. The term
“runoff” in particular is central to this work but is not well or consistently defined; it is interchangeably used
to describe meltwater, mobile water, and water that has left the ice sheet. In my book it is the latter only.
Elsewhere the term “rivers” is used but this is informal and not helpful; it would be better to make an
assessment of the intensity of meltwater flow in supraglacial channels and contrast the magnitude.
And it is stated in the abstract and repeated elsewhere that the amount of runoff from the percolation zone is
not known when this is simply not true – the authors used for example regional climate models that make an
estimate of this and there have been many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of ice
slabs on which this work is predicated. I would recommend a thorough parse of loose and hyperbolic
language.
We have endeavoured to tighten up our use of language throughout the manuscript, particularly around
the term ‘runoff’ which we agree was not used as precisely as it should have been. We hope that these changes
meet with approval.
The reviewer said that they find ‘too much hyperbole’. The only example they provided is: “it is stated in the
abstract and repeated elsewhere that the amount of runoff from the percolation zone is not known when this is
simply not true – the authors used for example regional climate models that make an estimate of this and there
have been many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of ice slabs on which this work is
predicated.”. Concerning this specific example, we disagree: regional climate models make estimates which
so far remain unvalidated for the percolation zone, especially where ice slabs are present. They are potentially
subject to major issues associated with invalid parameterisations. We currently have a manuscript co-written
with the MAR and RACMO teams under discussion which covers many of these themes in detail:
https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2024-2750. Nonetheless, to tighten the language we are happy to change
from ‘unknown’ to ‘unmeasured’, ‘unvalidated’. We also note that we have added further justification
for our heat flux modelling approach (over RCMs) in the Methods section ‘Modelling SIF’.
The reviewer states that there have been ‘many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of
ice slabs:
• The reviewer does not provide examples of these ‘many studies’.
• Taking this comment literally, we think the reviewer is suggesting that there are already several
studies of meltwater retention on top of ice slabs. We are not aware that such studies exist, with the
exceptions of already-cited studies of SIF atop glacier ice in the Canadian Arctic and Svalbard. In
Greenland, we are only aware of slab mapping/identification exercises, e.g. MacFerrin et al. (2019),
Jullien et al. (2023), Culberg et al. (2024), which do not simultaneously assess meltwater retention
processes.
• There is arguably perhaps one study, Machguth et al., (2016), which focuses on meltwater retention
on a slab. In this study, the term ‘superimposed ice formation’ appears only once, in the 3rd-last
paragraph of the Methods, only in reference to core alignment. This study undertook ‘barcode
alignment’ on a couple of firn cores at KAN_U, which as this reviewer points out subsequently can be
subject to substantial uncertainties. But having re-read this study in detail for this response we have
concluded that the evidence of SIF they present is so limited that we now do not cite it in the
Introduction as an observation of Greenland SIF.
2. Superimposed ice formation. The initial part of this work is based on in situ measurements that purport to
document superimposed ice formation. I am not persuaded that the authors have demonstrated this effectively.
The main approach is to measure the depth to the slab surface two years apart at a variety of locations. This is
not an actual measurement of superimposed ice formation, it’s a crude approximation. The slabs could be
mobile, because the site is not at the equilibrium line. More importantly, the authors are not able to resurvey
the same site and so their measurement is in fact a combination of spatial and temporal variation in slab
surface depth. Without knowing the former, it is impossible to deduce the latter. This calculation
unfortunately underpins the entire study, and so it is quite fundamental to convince the reader that the
measurements are robust. Having drilled many firn cores in this region I know that measuring the depth to a
common horizon is a very challenging thing to do with precision, and that there are typically large natural
variations in the depth of common horizons in any case. I wonder if repeat GPR would have been a better way
to do this entire experiment. Or drilling through the entire slab. Or analysing the core chemistry to isolate
annual layers. Certainly the spatial variation in slab surface depth needs to be reliable quantified somehow
before the temporal variation can be deduced.
We strongly disagree with the thrust of this comment that our in-situ observations are invalid. We highlight
that neither of the other two reviewers raised concerns of this nature. From our perspective there seems to
have been a misunderstanding of our field measurement protocol. At root, this seems to relate to the locations
at which we make our measurements. We do resurvey the same site between years: these locations are exactly
the same each year with respect to the underlying stratigraphy, as we returned to a location marked with a
bamboo stake. Each location had of course moved by several 10s of metres due to ice flow, but this process
does not affect the near surface stratigraphy. To clarify this further, we have improved our explanation,
including adding a supplementary figure which graphically illustrates the measurement process, and
supplementary discussion to discuss local variability in SIF more extensively.
In our judgement the suggestion of using GPR is a non-starter. If we were to make a GPR survey, we would
measure the thickness of the snow layer, albeit with larger uncertainty than by drilling. We ask ourselves: how
does GPR measure the thickness of the slab and in particular its annual growth? We could potentially detect
the bottom depth of the slab in subsequent years, but would be hampered by all the GPR-related uncertainties
that would reduce the precision of the outcome in such a study. And crucially, even if a change in thickness
could be measured beyond uncertainty, we still would not know whether the slab grew from accretion below
or above. In contrast, this is precisely what our approach of returning to a marked surface location in year 2
enables us to do.
The reviewer states “Having drilled so many firn cores in this region I know that measuring the depth to a
common horizon is very challenging…”. We have no way of assessing what expertise this reviewer has, nor
the scope of the region they are considering. The reviewer may have drilled firn cores at high elevations, but
perhaps not into ice slabs. Our cores are from the slabs, so are basically solid ice. In these cores, to say where
snow ends and firn starts is not always clear, but the horizon where the slab begins is always abundantly clear.
For more details, the core logs can be examined in our data repository.
3. Spatial variation in SIF. A main conclusion of this work is that the degree of superimposed ice formation is
higher closer to surface meltwater channels than it is distal from them. This is I think the most original aspect
of the study. However, the conclusion itself depends on how reliable the estimates of SIF (see point 2),
but
also on how strong the spatial correlation is. Looking at the data in Figure 1 I am not convinced that the
spatial variation in SIF is significantly correlated with the distribution of meltwater channels; there seem to be
just as many sites that buck the trend as there are that fit the hypothesis. The sites sampled are also quite
randomly distributed, which doesn’t help. Wouldn’t it make sense to survey a profile tangential to a channel,
for example? I think more work and quite possibly more data are needed to convince the reader that this
conclusion is robust.
As the reviewer notes, “the conclusion itself depends on how reliable the estimates of SIF (see point 2)” are.
As we respond above, we are confident in our SIF estimates and believe that there has been a
misunderstanding here.
Concerning spatial variation, Fig. 1 provides a high-level overview of the SIF magnitudes. Further evidence is
presented in Supplementary Figure 1, which explicitly compares the quantity of SIF with the Euclidean
distance to surface drainage visible on optical satellite imagery. Our measurements were concentrated on two
transects, with a spacing that reflects the proximity to surface drainage. Sites FS1, 122, camp, 231, 3u3
constitute one transect. The sites shown in Fig. 1d constitute another transect, which is quasi-tangential to the
main surface channel. We now note these transect configurations in the main text. Concerning a profile
truly tangential to a channel: the location of the channel varies somewhat between years, so this is less feasible
to deploy than it might first appear, and also what a transect equidistant of a stream is one year, would not be
the next. Concerning the measurement stations, these were installed to acquire data in three distinctively
different surface slope regimes and with contrasting surface hydrology in any given melt summer.
Please see also our response to reviewer 1 concerning possible spatial variability in melt.
4. Timing of SIF. There is a section of work on the timing of superimposed ice formation deduced from
measurements of the firn dielectric properties. I found this section very difficult to navigate and not
persuasive; the only thing that seems to be consistent about the probe measurements is how inconsistent they
are in time and space. It seems that very few measurements were actually made and yet apparently firm
conclusions are drawn from them. This is very similar to point 3; it suggests to me that the field experiment
was again not up to the task and in hindsight other measurements would have been made. It’s also not clear to
me how important it is to know the timing of superimposed ice formation – is that really material to this study
? My feeling is this whole is a distraction and could easily be dropped.
On reflection, we agree that knowing the sub-seasonal timing of SIF is not important to our key messages and
is challenging to interpret from our data. We have therefore removed this whole section as suggested.
5. Modelling. The study next leaps into a series of “model” experiments designed to help scale up the field
observations. However, these experiments are tangentially linked to the field measurements at best. The first
“model” is a physical 1D heat transfer model, the second is a linear regression between satellite radar
backscatter and measured superimposed ice formation, and the third is another linear regression between the
modelled superimposed ice formation and cumulative negative degree days derived (I think) from the 1D heat
transfer model. The heat flow model is very loosely related to the field observations as it is contrasted to
temperature profiles that are not directly related to the SIF. Moreover, we can’t really judge how well the
model and observations agree from the data as presented.
We are grateful for these comments, which together with similar comments by reviewer 2 caused us to
fundamentally rethink how we conduct our upscaling. We believe that we have now successfully
addressed this concern and that our response to reviewer 2 answers this major comment.
The satellite radar backscatter is very loosely related to in situ superimposed ice formation; many other factors
affect backscatter and in any case the correlation deduced is largely owing to the clustering of the
measurements into two distinct populations, without which there would be no correlation.
We recognise that in our previous submission there was the potential to conflate radar backscatter with in-situ
SIF, primarily because of the statistical way in which we attempted to conduct our upscaling; however, this
was not our intention. To be clear, we consider backscatter variations in autumn to tell us only about residual
wetness in the near-surface. It is the disappearance of this backscatter that we attribute to SIF, which we now
model physically instead of our previous problematic statistical approach. In the revised manuscript this is
now clearer because we talk only of residual wetness [duration] and not also in terms of sigmaHV0
backscatter strength like previously.
The degree of correlation between satellite derived SIF and negative degree days is relatively weak in any
case, half of the variation is not explained. I find this approach to be quite chaotic, highly empirical, and not
persuasive. I would recommend the authors rethink their approach here entirely and find a better way to add
context and value to their sparse field measurements. The authors do note that regional climate models with
coupled firn process models are another way to study meltwater retention and I agree this would be a better
way to approach this problem.
As explained in our response summary, we have taken heed of these concerns about the upscaling
approach and, we believe, now have a much better methodology with which to deliver our upscaled
calculations.
Concerning the suggestion here that RCMs with coupled firn process models would be a ‘better way’ to
approach the problem: we disagree, and also note that we do not state that they constitute a ‘better way’.
As we have tried to clarify in our re-submission, there are substantial uncertainties/problems remaining with how
RCMs and even observation-based SEB models represent the sub-surface, which makes it desirable to instead
adopt a simplified approach to modelling SIF. Please see in particular the Methods section ‘Modelling
superimposed ice formation’.
Minor comments
Line 1: I’m not sure the word rivers is helpful here as they are generally associated with land and rain fed. can
you describe in glaciological terminology instead?
The term ‘rivers’ is used elsewhere in the literature. Non exhaustive examples include line 2 of Yang and
Smith (2016, JGR); Smith et al. (2015, PNAS). We have decided to stick with this intuitive terminology rather
than ‘supraglacial streams and rivers’ at every mention.
Line 4: I don't think its unknown; there are estimates. need to be a bit clearer here what you mean
We have changed to ‘unmeasured’.
Line5: should probably be clear about what you mean by runoff; is it meltwater until it is mobile, or until it is
known that it will leave the ice sheet locus, or until it has left the ice sheet locus?
Here, in-line with the definition of runoff, water that is assumed to leave the ice sheet locus – updated to
refer to ‘visible runoff’ which is then linked to previous studies in the Introduction.
Line 6: I think you mean that up to 3/4 of the annual melt can be retained by SIF (i.e. the converse of what is
stated), or that the process of SIF can lead to meltwater being retained
We are a confused by this comment – the text said that ‘SIF….can retain up to roughly three quarters of
locally-produced annual melt’, which doesn’t seem the be converse. Nonetheless, we have tried to clarify in
our revised Abstract.
Line 7: Is the heat flow modelling informed somehow by the field observations? or how else are they linked?
This comment refers to the abstract. We have added a note that the modelling is initialised by in-situ field
observations. The full information is available in the main text as before.
Line 7: How are the SAR data used? would be helpful to state
We have added a note that they are used to derive residual wetness.
Line 8: Quantify "majority"
We prefer not to do this in the abstract, as while the numbers are always a majority (i.e. greater than half),
the
precise value depends on parameter choices. The reader should read the main text for these details.
Line 8: Quantify "remainder"
See previous comment.
Line 9: This probably answers my earlier point about the definition of runoff
Yes, we believe so; see also modified abstract.
Line 10: Using your model?
We are not sure what this comment refers to, sorry.
Line 11: Does this mean total or local SMB? not sure SMB is a good metric since it is the sum of
accumulation and ablation
This is a good point – we concur that SMB was a poor choice of metric. We now instead express this in
terms of runoff estimates made using Cryosat-2 altimetry measurements. We estimate that recent SIF
has decreased recent runoff by 2-3 %.
Line 12: Is there an uncertainty on 32 Gt?
This value has changed with our new upscaling approach; we now provide a ‘most-likely’ value (60 Gt)
together with a range (27-75 Gt). The range is primarily a function of which ice slab extent we examine, but
also varies depending on 10 m firn temperatures and autumn snowpack thickness.
Line 12: To call them hotspots this is relative to other areas, but it doesn’t seem that you have assessed those?
Considering refreezing in absolute terms (metres water equivalent), they are indeed hotspots compared to the
rest of the ice sheet. Nowhere else is this combination of (a) meltwater supply and (b) a snow/firn matrix in
which to refreeze onto the underlying ice met.
Line 19: Decreased not densified
Changed
Line 25: Is this really true? i think there are estimates in the models you are using- what I guess you are saying
is that they don't account for potential retention associated with the ice slabs. Thats very different to unknown
We have replaced with ‘unmeasured’.
Line 37: Running water not runoff
Changed
Line 40: Radar returns is not a jargon. Measurements?
We have changed to “measurements” as suggested, but note that this term has been used in the literature
previously (see for example MacFerrin et al. 2019 Supplementary).
Line 42: Technically the slabs themselves are superimposed ice and so yours are not the first observations
We are observing superimposed ice formation, i.e. the process of forming superimposed ice, as we state in the
text. Slab mapping has indeed already mapped superimposed ice.
Line 43: What is the runoff limit?
In lines 23-24 we now define the visible runoff limit alongside the visible runoff area.
Line 44: What is local runoff?
Changed to ‘net water discharge from the hydrological catchment’.
Fig 1: Why is fs1 high on both years?
That there was no slush field at the surface doesn’t mean that there was no slush beneath the surface. Visible
hydrological features do not tell the whole story, so we also need to look at the sub-surface. C-band SAR
clearly shows that this area remained wet for a long time after the end of the melt season (Fig. 5a, see wetter
feature between FS2 and downstream later, between 1730 and 1760 m asl).
Line 69: You are showing that the SIF varies by 10s of cm w e over short distances, so perhaps the smb does
too, let alone surface features? In which case you experiment is not well constrained
Please see our responses to reviewer 1 concerning surface melt rates.
Line 88: Why use e>3 when water is e=80?
The TDR measurements have been removed from this re-submission.
Line 94: TDR probe
The TDR measurements have been removed from this re-submission.
Fig.3 : It’s very difficult in this figure to contrast the observed and modelled temperature profiles, which seem
to be the only validation of the model. I suggest replotting them as e.g. a direct scatter plot with a colour
coding to illustrate depth so that we can see how well they compare (or otherwise)
We have redrawn this figure panel to make the comparisons between observed vs modelled temperature
profiles clearer. We have also added some text to the Results which addresses the offset between
observed and modelled profiles at the end of the melt season.
Line 139: Isn't this obviously the case? What else would be causing the SIF. I don't think this is a grand
conclusion
We are not exactly sure what `this’ refers to, as one sentence finishes and another starts at this line number.
Assuming that ‘this’ refers to the sentence in L137-139, we do not make out that this is a grand conclusion.
Rather, this statement supported the sentence which followed, i.e. ‘In contrast, larger amount of SIF can only
be explained by lateral transport of meltwater….’. We have made various minor changes to better explain
our model findings.
Line 141: Just because your model agrees with SIF in some places doesn't mean you can conclude that
something else must be happening elsewhere – that’s not a hypothesis you have tested by experiment. Is your
model able to simulate lateral movement of meltwater? What other processes might lead to local variations in
melting that are not simulated by your model? More work required here
The majority of cores show rather similar SIF. We clearly show that simulated background refreezing agrees
to SIF in several locations. It clearly does not agree in a few locations. We therefore looked for the reasons for
the disagreement. It is obvious that refreezing from only the melting directly above a given location cannot
vary so enormously in space given how homogeneous the snow-covered surface is and the rather small
elevation envelope that we worked within (see also our response to reviewer 1). We also observe the largest
refreezing rates where there is most slush. To us, it is logical that these locations should therefore have less
cold content in the slab. Finally, it is unclear to us what the benefit of including lateral movement in our 1-D
model would be.
Line 144: It does not indicate this; it just indicates you have a match within 1sigma in some locations
This line says ‘Since our model indicates that the localised larger quantities of superimposed ice cannot be
accommodated by slab cold content during the melt season alone…’.
Our model does indicate this as the modelled summertime SIF is valid for most of our measurement sites, not
just the one where we compare. Of course, we do not have more firn temperature data with which to undertake
a more thorough comparison. But in the context of how much larger some of SI measurements are (by
decimetres), then we consider a match within 1 sigma (0.06 m w.e.) sufficient for our assertions.
Line 156: Correlation, not relationship
This empirical parameterisation has been removed in this re-submission. Please see our response summary.
Fig. 4: These data are clustered in 2 populations which is leading to most of the correlation. I don't think they
are distributed well enough to develop an empirical parameterisation. why are they clustered in this way? I
suggest this is explored in more detail before jumping to conclusions
This empirical parameterisation has been removed in this re-submission. Please see our response summary.
Line 174: This is all a bit contrived; your result is entirely dependent upon the relationship that you force to
exist.
This empirical parameterisation has been removed in this re-submission. Please see our response summary.
Fig. 6: This isn't "wetness", its sigma nought. I think you are jumping to too many conclusions here
As we describe in the Methods, we derive a binary wetness indication by applying a threshold to detrended
sigma0HV. Thus, Figure 6 did present wetness (duration), not sigma0. This approach is based on
previously published work, most notably Liang et al. (2021). Note that Fig. 6 is now Suppl. Fig. 5.
Line 211: So only half of the variance is explained
This comment relates to the empirical parameterisation that has been removed in this re-submission.
Line 219: I'm lost here; if you have a model of the firn pack why are you counting cNDD to model SIF?
why
not just compute it from your actual model?
This comment relates to the empirical parameterisation that has been removed in this re-submission.
Line 334: Such as?
We now summarise the specific issues (difficulty locating the slab surface at FS3; uncertainty related to
drilling into SIF until metal chips appeared).
Line 336: Why are they minimum estimates?
Please see response to previous comment.
Line 343: This is a poorly constrained experiment as you don't know the spatial variation in firn stratigraphy.
how can you be sure you are measuring superimposed ice?
We believe that this concern is addressed by our more detailed explanation of our field measurement
protocol and Supplementary Discussion; specifically, during our repeat measurements, we found very little
spatial variability at metres scales.
Line 358: So this is an underestimtae of the SIF?
This paragraph is about the cSMB, not about SIF. By definition (Cogley et al. 2011), SIF refers only to
refreezing on top of impermeable horizons, in this case the ice slab.
Line 459: Why choose the 1st percentile? is this based on theory?
Please see our response to Reviewer 2.
Line 461: Why likely?
Thanks for pointing this out – on reflection, we do not think we can quantify this statement that the threshold
is ‘likely conservative’, so have removed it in this re-submission.
Line 466: Extrapolate or scale up, not distribute
This comment relates to the empirical parameterisation that has been removed in this re-submission.
Line 470: This isn't determining the existence of a relationship, it is assuming the existence of a relationship
This comment relates to the empirical parameterisation that has been removed in this re-submission.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Tedstone et al, 2024
Summary
This paper uses a combination of field observations, satellite observations, and simple/conceptual modelling to address the important topic of meltwater retention in the percolation zone of the Greenland ice sheet – about which there is some uncertainty. The paper builds on the finding that meltwater retention has led to the formation of ice slabs at depth the firn pack, and that the presence of these slabs disrupts the normal process of meltwater percolation and redistribution.
The paper is quite challenging to comprehend as it contains several elements of work that are not easily linked and are each quite obscure. Despite several attempts to read and review, I could not form a clear narrative from the study and, more importantly, I was not persuaded by the arguments presented. Either the narrative needs to be strengthened, or the arguments need to be made more compelling with further work.
Major
I have identified five major concerns that I hope will act as a guide for the authors to reformulate their paper.
1. Loose language. There is lots of loose language and (for me) too much hyperbole in this paper. The term “runoff” in particular is central to this work but is not well or consistently defined; it is interchangeably used to describe meltwater, mobile water, and water that has left the ice sheet. In my book it is the latter only. Elsewhere the term “rivers” is used but this is informal and not helpful; it would be better to make an assessment of the intensity of meltwater flow in supraglacial channels and contrast the magnitude. And it is stated in the abstract and repeated elsewhere that the amount of runoff from the percolation zone is not known when this is simply not true – the authors used for example regional climate models that make an estimate of this and there have been many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of ice slabs on which this work is predicated. I would recommend a thorough parse of loose and hyperbolic language.
2. Superimposed ice formation. The initial part of this work is based on in situ measurements that purport to document superimposed ice formation. I am not persuaded that the authors have demonstrated this effectively. The main approach is to measure the depth to the slab surface two years apart at a variety of locations. This is not an actual measurement of superimposed ice formation, it’s a crude approximation. The slabs could be mobile, because the site is not at the equilibrium line. More importantly, the authors are not able to resurvey the same site and so their measurement is in fact a combination of spatial and temporal variation in slab surface depth. Without knowing the former, it is impossible to deduce the latter. This calculation unfortunately underpins the entire study, and so it is quite fundamental to convince the reader that the measurements are robust. Having drilled many firn cores in this region I know that measuring the depth to a common horizon is a very challenging thing to do with precision, and that there are typically large natural variations in the depth of common horizons in any case. I wonder if repeat GPR would have been a better way to do this entire experiment. Or drilling through the entire slab. Or analysing the core chemistry to isolate annual layers. Certainly the spatial variation in slab surface depth needs to be reliable quantified somehow before the temporal variation can be deduced.
3. Spatial variation in SIF. A main conclusion of this work is that the degree of superimposed ice formation is higher closer to surface meltwater channels than it is distal from them. This is I think the most original aspect of the study. However, the conclusion itself depends on how reliable the estimates of SIF (see point 2), but also on how strong the spatial correlation is. Looking at the data in Figure 1 I am not convinced that the spatial variation in SIF is significantly correlated with the distribution of meltwater channels; there seem to be just as many sites that buck the trend as there are that fit the hypothesis. The sites sampled are also quite randomly distributed, which doesn’t help. Wouldn’t it make sense to survey a profile tangential to a channel, for example? I think more work and quite possibly more data are needed to convince the reader that this conclusion is robust.
4. Timing of SIF. There is a section of work on the timing of superimposed ice formation deduced from measurements of the firn dielectric properties. I found this section very difficult to navigate and not persuasive; the only thing that seems to be consistent about the probe measurements is how inconsistent they are in time and space. It seems that very few measurements were actually made and yet apparently firm conclusions are drawn from them. This is very similar to point 3; it suggests to me that the field experiment was again not up to the task and in hindsight other measurements would have been made. It’s also not clear to me how important it is to know the timing of superimposed ice formation – is that really material to this study ? My feeling is this whole is a distraction and could easily be dropped.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to reviews
Concurrent superimposed ice formation and meltwater
runoff on Greenland’s ice slabs, version 1
Summary
We thank the three reviewers for their engagement with our first submission. We believe that we have
successfully addressed their major concerns, leading to major improvements which warrant re-submission
through the Nature Communications appeals process.
Reviewer 1 found the manuscript to be well-written, thorough, and provide important observational evidence.
Their concerns were essentially minor. The bulk of our changes concern comments by reviewers 2 and 3.
Reviewer 2 said that the manuscript addresses an important caveat to the popular notion that ice slabs lead to
runoff. They found the field measurements novel and convincing but were concerned that the remote sensing
analysis had poorly quantified but likely large uncertainties. Reviewer 3 had some major concerns about both
the field measurements and the upscaling.
Our most major and important changes are:
1. We have developed a new upscaling methodology. We no longer rely on statistical links between
field-measured SIF, negative degree days and SAR. Instead, we extend our physical heat flux
modelling approach to estimate SIF through (a) ‘bottom-up’ (i.e. slab cold content) refreezing during
both summer and autumn, and (b) ‘top-down’ refreezing (i.e. negative air temperatures) during
autumn. We still use SAR sigma0HV, but only to determine wetness duration both across the field
area and ice-slabs-wide through application of a binary threshold. We undertake these calculations in
both our field area and ice-slabs-wide. It also allows a much more rigorous exploration of
uncertainties. In our view this is a more elegant and physical approach, particularly because it allows
us to fully differentiate between summer and autumn SIF. Please see our headline response to
reviewer 2 for more details.
2. Our ice-slabs-wide analysis now incorporates the new ice slab extents mapped by Culberg et al.
(2024); as these extents are much larger than Jullien et al. (2023), our estimate of SIF onto ice slabs
has increased accordingly.
3. We have recomputed our SAR wetness threshold and we have examined the sensitivity of our
calculations to the choice of the SAR sigma0HV threshold for mapping wetness; our findings are
robust across the specified sensitivity range of the Sentinel-1 SAR sensor.
4. We disagree with the view of reviewer 3 that our in-situ stake measurements of SI are insufficient to
demonstrate our purported findings. In response we have extended our description of our SIF
measurement protocol, including the addition of a sketch figure to the supplementary materials. Please
also see the rebuttal in this response document. We do however agree that our measurements to
capture SIF timing are not fully convincing, so have removed these accordingly.
5. We have made many improvements to the main text which we hope improve the readability.
Our changes in bold
In our longer responses, the key parts are underlined.
This manuscript presents estimates of superimposed ice formation on top of ice slabs along the K-Transect in
SW Greenland. In this study, the authors present field measurements that suggest local ice formation on ice
slabs can retain ¾ of local annual surface melt. They estimate that ice formation along ice slabs facilitated the
retention of ~32 gigatonnes of melt between 2017 and 2022, roughly ~4% of the Greenland SMB.
Overall, the manuscript is well-written, thorough, and presents important observational evidence for surface
melt refreeze onto ice slabs, which plays a role on the overall SMB of the GrIS. I have several comments,
most of which are relatively minor; I believe that their consideration will overall improve the manuscript.
I have organized the comments below, grouped by section within the manuscript.
Results:
Pg 3 line 77: Because local melt is near uniform across the study area (presumably as a result of their
modeling results, but this is not made explicit), they hypothesis that measured spatial variation in SIF is
indicative of inputs not only from local melt production, but also lateral water flow. This seems entirely
reasonable given the observed increases in SIF for sites proximal to major surface rivers. However, the
inclusion of external references to reinforce this claim would be beneficial.
As the reviewer infers, we take melt as a smoothly varying field of decreasing melt with increasing elevation,
as calculated by a surface energy balance model forced by in-situ observations. Fig 5d now illustrates how
melt decreases with increasing elevation. We also now refer to findings from Noel et al. 2016 in the first
paragraph of our Results. They showed that melt rates show very little spatial variability in this region.
It is possible that, once visible slush fields have developed, then local melt rates might increase further as a
function of their reduced albedo. However, these slush fields can only initially develop by the transport and
ponding of melt that is essentially uniform in space considering the smooth surface topography over 100s
metres scales and homogeneous snow surface cover (e.g. Holmes 1955; Noel et al., 2016; Clerx et al., 2024/in
press). In other words, their origin does not lie in albedo. Nonetheless, we now note this possibility of
subsequent local melt enhancement in the first paragraph of the Discussion.
Page 4 line 79: “Finally, beyond 2–4 km away from visible surface runoff, we found that SIF began to
increase again, as illustrated by 0.25 m w.e. at site 3u3 (Suppl. Fig. 1).” – With what degree of confidence can
this claim be made, given that it is reliant upon a single point wise measurement of SIF, and the measured
value is within 2 standard deviations of the reported average SIF from 2022?
On reflection, we agree, so we have removed this statement from the main text.
Page 7 line 139: “In contrast, larger amounts of SIF can only be explained by lateral transport of meltwater
which provides additional water for SIF to continue in specific locations beyond the end of the melt season.” –
Similar to first comment; Isn’t it possible that this elevated SIF can also be explained by spatial heterogeneity
in melt that is not captured in the SMB model? I tend to agree with the authors that the more plausible
explanation is lateral transport of meltwater, but to what degree can spatial heterogeneity of melt be ruled out?
Please see our response to the previous comment about spatial variability in melt.
An important point to mention in the refreezing during Autumn section is the role that volume scattering due
to surface and subsurface heterogeneities (e.g. surface roughness, sastrugi, ice lenses, ice pipes, percolation
pipes) plays. Implicitly, the bias-removal approach that is employed here *should* account for this process,
provided the geometry of these features is assumed temporally non-varying, such that changes in the cross-
polarization backscatter can be attributed solely to changes in dielectric permittivity rather than surface
roughness and volume scattering. I would suggest that this point be elaborated upon in the methods section,
2
perhaps with reference to some relevant literature (e.g., Rignot 1995, Backscatter Model for the Unusual
Radar Properties of the Greenland Ice Sheet).
Thanks for this suggestion. We have elaborated in the Methods (‘Detecting residual water presence’)
accordingly.
Methods:
Page 16, line 396: Regarding the model producing 0.25 m w.e. melt; is this merely a consequence of the
subsurface model discretization being 0.25 m? If not, what is the uncertainty of this model-derived estimate of
w.e. melt?
No, this is not a consequence of the sub-surface model discretisation. In each time step, the model’s grid
moves up/down after the occurrence of accumulation/ablation; van As et al. (2017) contains full details.
Concerning uncertainty: the model does not come with uncertainty bounds because of the complex and non-
linear nature of the modelling. This makes validation a crucial aspect of SEB modelling, as is done in
numerous previous studies. Concerning this model specifically, see e.g. van As et al. (2017) cited in
manuscript. In this manuscript we therefore evaluate how sensible its melt estimates are by reference to in-situ
surface lowering measurements, which show excellent agreement (see Methods).
Page 18 line 469: Section on the linear regression between measured SIF and mean crosspol backscatter:
given that an uncertainty in the in situ SIF values are provided, it would be worthwhile to propagate this
uncertainty through the linear regression for a nominal uncertainty estimate of the linearly-regressed area-
wide SIF estimates, particularly since the R2 in the linear regression isn’t particularly strong.
The linear regression approach has been removed in this re-submission.
This manuscript describes field measurements of superimposed ice formation on top of ice slabs on
Greenland’s K-transect in the summers of 2021 and 2022. Using repeated firn cores, time domain
reflectometry, and thermal modeling, the authors show that a significant portion of annual melt refreezes on
top of the ice slabs due to ice slab cold content and cold surface temperatures during autumn. In particular, the
authors show that refreezing occurs even where water flows laterally over the surface, potentially for kms,
suggesting that surface mass loss may not scale directly with visible surface runoff during the melt season.
The authors then use Sentinel-1 SAR measurements to establish relationships between their field
measurements of SIF and radar-inferred surface wetness measurements. They use these relationships to scale
their SIF measurements first to the area surrounding their field site and then to the entire ice sheet. The
authors conclude that SIF accounts for about 4% of the contemporary GrIS SMB, making it a small but non-
trivial contributor to the overall ice sheet mass balance.
Overall, this paper addresses an important caveat to the popular notion that ice slabs lead to complete surface
runoff. In particular, the field measurements are novel and convincing and suggest that superimposed ice
formation (SIF) needs to be accounted for in order to understand how quickly surface melting becomes mass
loss as melting advances inland on the ice sheet. However, the remote sensing analyses used to scale these
field measurements to the entire ice sheet are subject to large uncertainties, many of which are not well
quantified in the current manuscript. I am particularly concerned that the approach to estimating pan-
Greenland SIF relies on a highly uncertain relationship between SIF and nCDD in a single ~30 km x 30 km
region which cannot be validated anywhere else on the ice sheet, as well a background SIF rate that is
assumed to not vary at all across the ice sheet. This opens the potential for large, uncharacterizable regional
biases to affect the pan-Greenland SIF estimates.
‘[the authors use a] background SIF rate that is assumed to not vary at all across the ice sheet’. In fact, the
background SIF rate used for the ice-slabs-wide analysis varies in two ways:
(1) As in our first submission, our treatment of the conditions which permit SIF across the ice sheet is
explicitly spatial. At a given MAR model grid node, SIF can only occur during the melt season and
when the slab is covered in (porous) snow which provides the basis for a slush matrix overlying the
slab.
(2) Previously, we used three different fixed initial temperature scenarios to model bottom-up summer
SIF. In this re-submission, we instead use the state-of-the-art ice-sheet-wide 10 m depth
temperatures data product published by Vandecrux et al. (2024, TC) to initialise our bottom-up
SIF modelling. We also run our model at +/- the stated uncertainty of the Vandecrux product.
We consider this to be a major improvement compared to the previous version of our manuscript.
Concerning the remote sensing analyses: we concur with the reviewer’s concerns that these were subject to
large uncertainties and had the potential for large, uncharacterizable regional biases to affect the pan-GrIS SIF
estimates. In conjunction with similar concerns raised by reviewer 3, we have therefore made major
revisions which replace the previous statistical approach completely with physical heat flow modelling
to make our upscaling calculations. In summary:
(1) In areas which remain wet after the end of the melt season according to SAR, we now allow our
summertime “bottom-up” calculations to continue into autumn until SAR indicates that the area is
dry, yielding the additional bottom-up SIF which occurs in autumn. We partition the contributions of
summer vs autumn bottom-up SIF using the last day of melting from passive microwave radiometry.
(2) In these same areas, we now also explicitly address “top-down” refreezing as a result of negative
surface temperatures, beginning once the melt season has finished. These calculations are very
sensitive to the thickness of the snowpack overlying the slush matrix; we discuss this further in the
manuscript.
(3) Any pixels suspected of being lakes (i.e. still ‘residually wet’ at the end of the year) are now
completely excluded from our calculations.
(4) We have recalculated the SAR sensitivity threshold using data acquired in all areas labelled as
‘minimum likely’ slabs by Culberg et al. (2024, TC), with little resulting change (see below).
4
(5) Over our field area, we now show the uncertainty in our SIF calculations associated with the stated
sensitivity of the Sentinel-1 SAR sensor used to determine wetness duration. We show that this source
of uncertainty is second order, i.e. wetness duration does not change appreciably within this
sensitivity range. We also checked this on an ice-slabs-wide basis where again it is a second-order
source of uncertainty (see Supplementary Figure 4).
Major Comments:
[1] I am a bit confused about the primary purpose of modelling of the rate of superimposed ice formation. The
authors state that the reason they conduct the modelling is to determine the degree to which ice slab warming
is due to latent heating. If this is indeed the main goal, then the argument would be better supported by
comparing the model run presented in the paper to a model run forced by the measured surface temperature
and which only considers heat conduction (no latent heating). The difference between those two scenarios
would provide a stronger quantification of the role of latent heating in warming the ice slabs.
However, the primary conclusion that seems to come out of this section is that refreezing due
to ice slab cold content can only account for measured SIF rates in regions without additional
advection of meltwater. If the goal is instead to accurately model local SIF, then it seems like the authors
might be better served by using their fully coupled SEB-firn model instead of this simplified model that
imposes a fixed meltwater supply that may or may not be consistent with the actual melt supply and timing
during the season when measurements were made.
We agree that we should have been clearer here. Our main goal was neither to super-accurately model local
SIF nor to determine the degree to which ice slab warming is due to latent heating. Rather, it was to provide a
constraint on how much SIF can occur during the melt season under the plausible assumption of a continuous
meltwater supply at the slab surface. Then, SIF in excess of this logically occurs during autumn, i.e. after
active surface melt has finished. In other words, the primary purpose of this modelling approach is to partition
the SIF that we measured into the melt and post-melt seasons, thereby setting the scene for a slabs-wide first-
order estimate of SIF later in the study. With our revised modelling approach we believe that this is
motivation is much clearer.
An ideal solution would indeed be to use a fully coupled SEB-firn model. However, no such model that is
suitable for our application exists. We are dealing with the problem of ponded meltwater in a snow matrix
atop an impermeable and cold barrier, which is an extreme end-member of what can be considered ‘firn’. We
understand from firn modelling colleagues that even when ponding subroutines are available then they often
remain disabled for want of validation. We now describe these issues in the Methods section ‘Modelling
SIF’. Thus, it is more informative to simplify the problem as far as possible, i.e. by considering a relatively
thin snowpack with a continuously wet slush matrix on top of an ice slab (conditions which were met for
much of the melt season according to our in-situ measurements and further bolstered by observations in Clerx
et al., 2022) and then using classical heat flux theory to determine the rate of refreezing at first order.
New in this re-submission is an alternative configuration of the model to estimate SIF caused by
atmospheric cooling (‘top-down’). As we describe in the paper, an issue here is that we lack good bounds on
the thickness of the snowpack overlying the slush matrix. We wanted to use end-of-season snowpack
thickness simulated by MAR but found that the outputs were highly spatially incoherent, which is a further
caution against 'blind’ use of RCMs assuming that they always deliver the best results. The reviewer may be
interested to see a paper with several of the same co-authors as this submission currently in Discussion, which
describes some of the difficulties with RCM behaviour at the runoff limits (https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-
2024-2750).
Overall, we contend that our chosen approach is much simpler to interpret than the outputs of a fully coupled
SEB-firn model. In turn, we hope that our findings can be used to advance ponding schemes in firn models.
We have made narrative changes to the relevant parts of the manuscript accordingly.
5
[2] Uncertainty in the regression between measured SIF and the multi-temporal mean 𝜎̂ 𝐻𝑉 can be better
quantified and mapped into uncertainty in the study site SIF map (Fig. 4b). One option would be to use a
Bayesian regression that can quantify the range of linear models that are consistent with the data. This would
make it possible to produce an uncertainty map showing the range of the plausible SIF for each pixel in Fig.
4b given the range of plausible models. But the key point is that there should be corresponding uncertainty
map for Fig 4b that account for uncertainty in the SIF-𝜎̂ 𝐻𝑉 relationship and the uncertainty in the background
SIF rate.
Similarly, better uncertainty quantification is needed for the SIF-nCDD regression. Particularly given the
relatively poor R2 value for this regression, I strongly feel that it is important to quantify the uncertainty in the
model fit and clearly demonstrate how that uncertainty maps onto uncertainty in the final estimates of regional
autumn SIF that are presented in Figure 7.
This analysis has been removed from our re-submission.
[3] For setting the SAR wetness backscatter threshold, I would like to see some sensitivity tests from different
regions of the ice sheet showing how the 1st percentile of 𝜎̂ 𝐻𝑉 prior to the melt season varies regionally. For
a reliable pan-Greenland mapping, it is very important to establish whether conditions in SW Greenland are
consistent across the ice sheet. Other studies that have used Sentinel-1 data to quantify either melting or the
extent of wet snow facies over Greenland have found that performance with a single threshold can vary
significantly across the ice sheet (Hu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023). Regional bias due to a fixed wetness
threshold should be quantified and incorporated into assessments of overall uncertainty.
We thank the reviewer for raising these concerns. First, we comment on the literature citations:
(1) The findings of Hu et al. 2022 are not as relevant to our study as they first appear. Hu et al. did not
normalise summertime retrievals with respect to winter, unlike in our current approach, and so
therefore a considerable source of variability remains.
(2) Li et al. 2024’s methodology is more similar to ours. They emphasise that SAR-based mapping of
wetness at a set threshold is only reliable above the snowline, but that there is no appreciable regional
variability above the snowline. As we consider only snow-covered surfaces above the ELA, the
difficulties that Li et al. experienced with selecting a threshold applicable to melt detection over bare
ice is not relevant here.
We recap that our threshold of -2.1 dB was quite similar to Liang et al. 2021, who rather than the 1st percentile
take the less conservative 5th percentile of dry snow as their threshold: -2.66 dB. Both Liang et al., 2021 and
Li et al. 2024 employ a more conservative value of -3 dB, +/- 0.3 dB, but they had the express aim of
capturing surface melting conditions which they validated by reference to in-situ air temperature
measurements. This is not a relevant validation metric in our case as we are seeking to identify residual
wetness after the end of active melt, which also indicates that a 3 dB threshold would be too conservative for
our purposes here.
Notwithstanding this comparison, we have undertaken another examination of our threshold choice. Now, we
compute histograms by sampling all areas within the ‘minimum likely ice slab’ classification of Culberg
et al. (2024), rather than just the western flank of the ice sheet as previously. The 1st percentile value
has decreased slightly to -1.17 dB (i.e. 0.07 dB more conservative than in our previous submission).
In the revised manuscript we adopt the new threshold of -1.17 dB, +- 0.3 dB indicative of the
radiometric uncertainty of Sentinel-1’s sensor as per Geudtner and Torres (2012). We use the +/- to
propagate an uncertainty in wetness duration through to our final calculations in our field area. On an
ice-slabs-wide basis, we provide a new Supplementary Figure which shows that the residual wetness
duration/area is essentially insensitive to the radiometric uncertainty of the sensor.
[4] I am concerned about how well the nCDD model can be generalized to map autumn SIF rates across the
entire ice sheet. This is conceptually quite similar to the positive degree day model used for melting, which
has a spatially and temporally variable rate factor that typically needs to be tuned for individual sites. I have
similar concerns for the nCDD model. Essentially, the authors’ scaling assumes that air temperature is the
only driver of refreezing and neglects all the other components of the subsurface energy balance, to include
firn and snow conditions, which might vary significantly across the ice sheet. It also assumes that the amount
of melt that is refrozen scales directly with the length of time required to fully refreeze an area, which may be
generally reasonable, but would absolutely be influenced by the transient accumulation rate, subsurface
temperatures, etc on the local scale. Without secondary validation sites, it seems basically impossible to know
if the regression model coefficients will apply anywhere outside of southwest Greenland.
This analysis has been removed from our re-submission.
[5] How are buried lakes accounted for when calculating autumn SIF? If I have understood the methods
correctly, it seems like there has been no attempt to separate that mode of water
impoundment from superimposed ice formation. It seems problematic to apply a relationship
between nCDD and refreezing in porous snow or a slush matrix to the refreezing of large open water bodies.
Since buried lakes will have the highest and most persistent wetness values (see the authors’ own Figure 5,
which is dominated by lakes), I am concerned that including lakes may significantly bias the results.
Thanks for raising this concern. Now, we screen out likely lakes by removing pixels which are still wet in
the last SAR acquisition each calendar year.
Minor Comments:
Overall, the section titles and introductory sentences could do a better job of explaining to the reader
the end goal of the analyses being described in the section. For example, the section “Modelling the rate of
superimposed ice formation” would be easier to follow if it started with a sentence explaining why the authors
want to model this quantity. The section title could also better reflect the findings instead of the methods, for
example, something like “Ice slab cold content a key factor in summer SIF”.
Thanks for this suggestion. We have made several changes accordingly.
Line 34 – I am not sure I understand what the second half of this sentence is trying to express.
We have rephrased as we agree that this was very unclear previously.
Line 92 – Why was there no spike in 𝜖 when this water reached and fully flooded the probe before refreezing?
We cannot know for sure, but as the section ‘Timing of SIF’ has been removed in response to reviewer 3
concerns, we have not investigated further.
Line 185/296 – there are now estimates of ice slab extent from both modeling (Brils et al., 2024) and Sentinel-
1 observations (Culberg et al., 2024) that provide a more up-to-date and comprehensive outline of ice slab
extent on the GrIS.
Indeed - though we find it a little concerning that literature published in 2023 can already be considered less
‘up-to-date’! Nonetheless, given that we have made major changes to our upscaling approach, we have taken
the opportunity to replace the Jullien et al. (2023) outlines with those based on Sentinel-1 observations
by Culberg et al. (2024). We now explore the impact that the uncertainty in ice slab extent makes on our final
estimates of SIF.
We have moved the statements of ice slab extent previously found at this location into the Introduction.
would at least provide a constraint on the shape and range of temperature profiles in ice slab regions.
Thanks for this suggestion. Rather than using modelled temperature profiles for initialisation with all the
uncertainties in RCM sub-surface schemes, we take advantage of another study that has been published this
year: Vandecrux et al. (2024, TC), which mapped observed 10 m depth temperatures ice-sheet-wide using
machine learning techniques, presented along with an associated uncertainty product. We use the Vandecrux
data to set the bottom temperature of our initial temperature profiles and then scale our observed
profile from FS2 accordingly. We also run our calculations +/- the stated 10 m temperature uncertainty.
Please see our revised Methods section for more information.
How is the long-term equilibrium line in Figure 5 defined?
This was based on RACMO data 1981-2000. But in this re-submission we have modified this figure to only
show wetness in the Culberg et al. (2024) maximum ice slabs extent area.
Line 297 – I found the context for the discussion future warming and peak refreezing a bit confusing. Is the
point simply that we should not project current SIF rates as a function of SMB into the future due to the
uncertainty in climate forcing and hypsometry?
We have made efforts to improve the narrative of this paragraph – please see full text.
Line 476 – where did n=4 come from when only 3 PROMICE weather stations were noted in the study area?
Which stations were used and how are they distributed in elevation across the study area? (e.g. is it fully
representative of the elevation distribution, or does this scaling do significant extrapolation outside the data
bounds?)
The middle and upper weather stations largely encompass our study area, with the upper station being situated
at 1840 m ASL. Above this elevation SEB model input variables are extrapolated, not interpolated, and
therefore calculations do not exceed 2000 m ASL so that extrapolation does not become unrealistic. The
model uses these observations to compute in discrete 100 m elevation bins. We computed our regression
across four elevation bins (1,600, 1700, 1800 and 1,900 m asl). This was not clear previously, so thanks for
drawing this to our attention and we have updated the text accordingly.
Line 506 – What determines if a cell becomes snow free? Is this from MAR, an albedo remote sensing
product, or something else?
According to modelled MAR snowpack. This is now noted in the text.
Line 526 – wouldn’t a brief rise above 0C potentially lead to melting that could supply more water for SIF?
We have added a note that, given several weeks of prior atmospheric cooling of the snowpack, it is probable
that this melt would simply have been refrozen in the uppermost centimetres below the surface.
Summary
This paper uses a combination of field observations, satellite observations, and simple/conceptual modelling
to address the important topic of meltwater retention in the percolation zone of the Greenland ice sheet –
about which there is some uncertainty. The paper builds on the finding that meltwater retention has led to the
formation of ice slabs at depth the firn pack, and that the presence of these slabs disrupts the normal process of
meltwater percolation and redistribution.
The paper is quite challenging to comprehend as it contains several elements of work that are not easily linked
and are each quite obscure. Despite several attempts to read and review, I could not form a clear narrative
from the study and, more importantly, I was not persuaded by the arguments presented. Either the narrative
needs to be strengthened, or the arguments need to be made more compelling with further work.
Major
I have identified five major concerns that I hope will act as a guide for the authors to reformulate their paper.
1. Loose language. There is lots of loose language and (for me) too much hyperbole in this paper. The term
“runoff” in particular is central to this work but is not well or consistently defined; it is interchangeably used
to describe meltwater, mobile water, and water that has left the ice sheet. In my book it is the latter only.
Elsewhere the term “rivers” is used but this is informal and not helpful; it would be better to make an
assessment of the intensity of meltwater flow in supraglacial channels and contrast the magnitude.
And it is stated in the abstract and repeated elsewhere that the amount of runoff from the percolation zone is
not known when this is simply not true – the authors used for example regional climate models that make an
estimate of this and there have been many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of ice
slabs on which this work is predicated. I would recommend a thorough parse of loose and hyperbolic
language.
We have endeavoured to tighten up our use of language throughout the manuscript, particularly around
the term ‘runoff’ which we agree was not used as precisely as it should have been. We hope that these changes
meet with approval.
The reviewer said that they find ‘too much hyperbole’. The only example they provided is: “it is stated in the
abstract and repeated elsewhere that the amount of runoff from the percolation zone is not known when this is
simply not true – the authors used for example regional climate models that make an estimate of this and there
have been many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of ice slabs on which this work is
predicated.”. Concerning this specific example, we disagree: regional climate models make estimates which
so far remain unvalidated for the percolation zone, especially where ice slabs are present. They are potentially
subject to major issues associated with invalid parameterisations. We currently have a manuscript co-written
with the MAR and RACMO teams under discussion which covers many of these themes in detail:
https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2024-2750. Nonetheless, to tighten the language we are happy to change
from ‘unknown’ to ‘unmeasured’, ‘unvalidated’. We also note that we have added further justification
for our heat flux modelling approach (over RCMs) in the Methods section ‘Modelling SIF’.
The reviewer states that there have been ‘many studies on meltwater retention including the identification of
ice slabs:
• The reviewer does not provide examples of these ‘many studies’.
• Taking this comment literally, we think the reviewer is suggesting that there are already several
studies of meltwater retention on top of ice slabs. We are not aware that such studies exist, with the
exceptions of already-cited studies of SIF atop glacier ice in the Canadian Arctic and Svalbard. In
Jullien et al. (2023), Culberg et al. (2024), which do not simultaneously assess meltwater retention
processes.
• There is arguably perhaps one study, Machguth et al., (2016), which focuses on meltwater retention
on a slab. In this study, the term ‘superimposed ice formation’ appears only once, in the 3rd-last
paragraph of the Methods, only in reference to core alignment. This study undertook ‘barcode
alignment’ on a couple of firn cores at KAN_U, which as this reviewer points out subsequently can be
subject to substantial uncertainties. But having re-read this study in detail for this response we have
concluded that the evidence of SIF they present is so limited that we now do not cite it in the
Introduction as an observation of Greenland SIF.
2. Superimposed ice formation. The initial part of this work is based on in situ measurements that purport to
document superimposed ice formation. I am not persuaded that the authors have demonstrated this effectively.
The main approach is to measure the depth to the slab surface two years apart at a variety of locations. This is
not an actual measurement of superimposed ice formation, it’s a crude approximation. The slabs could be
mobile, because the site is not at the equilibrium line. More importantly, the authors are not able to resurvey
the same site and so their measurement is in fact a combination of spatial and temporal variation in slab
surface depth. Without knowing the former, it is impossible to deduce the latter. This calculation
unfortunately underpins the entire study, and so it is quite fundamental to convince the reader that the
measurements are robust. Having drilled many firn cores in this region I know that measuring the depth to a
common horizon is a very challenging thing to do with precision, and that there are typically large natural
variations in the depth of common horizons in any case. I wonder if repeat GPR would have been a better way
to do this entire experiment. Or drilling through the entire slab. Or analysing the core chemistry to isolate
annual layers. Certainly the spatial variation in slab surface depth needs to be reliable quantified somehow
before the temporal variation can be deduced.
We strongly disagree with the thrust of this comment that our in-situ observations are invalid. We highlight
that neither of the other two reviewers raised concerns of this nature. From our perspective there seems to
have been a misunderstanding of our field measurement protocol. At root, this seems to relate to the locations
at which we make our measurements. We do resurvey the same site between years: these locations are exactly
the same each year with respect to the underlying stratigraphy, as we returned to a location marked with a
bamboo stake. Each location had of course moved by several 10s of metres due to ice flow, but this process
does not affect the near surface stratigraphy. To clarify this further, we have improved our explanation,
including adding a supplementary figure which graphically illustrates the measurement process, and
supplementary discussion to discuss local variability in SIF more extensively.
In our judgement the suggestion of using GPR is a non-starter. If we were to make a GPR survey, we would
measure the thickness of the snow layer, albeit with larger uncertainty than by drilling. We ask ourselves: how
does GPR measure the thickness of the slab and in particular its annual growth? We could potentially detect
the bottom depth of the slab in subsequent years, but would be hampered by all the GPR-related uncertainties
that would reduce the precision of the outcome in such a study. And crucially, even if a change in thickness
could be measured beyond uncertainty, we still would not know whether the slab grew from accretion below
or above. In contrast, this is precisely what our approach of returning to a marked surface location in year 2
enables us to do.
The reviewer states “Having drilled so many firn cores in this region I know that measuring the depth to a
common horizon is very challenging…”. We have no way of assessing what expertise this reviewer has, nor
the scope of the region they are considering. The reviewer may have drilled firn cores at high elevations, but
perhaps not into ice slabs. Our cores are from the slabs, so are basically solid ice. In these cores, to say where
snow ends and firn starts is not always clear, but the horizon where the slab begins is always abundantly clear.
For more details, the core logs can be examined in our data repository.
3. Spatial variation in SIF. A main conclusion of this work is that the degree of superimposed ice formation is
higher closer to surface meltwater channels than it is distal from them. This is I think the most original aspect
of the study. However, the conclusion itself depends on how reliable the estimates of SIF (see point 2), but
also on how strong the spatial correlation is. Looking at the data in Figure 1 I am not convinced that the
spatial variation in SIF is significantly correlated with the distribution of meltwater channels; there seem to be
just as many sites that buck the trend as there are that fit the hypothesis. The sites sampled are also quite
randomly distributed, which doesn’t help. Wouldn’t it make sense to survey a profile tangential to a channel,
for example? I think more work and quite possibly more data are needed to convince the reader that this
conclusion is robust.
As the reviewer notes, “the conclusion itself depends on how reliable the estimates of SIF (see point 2)” are.
As we respond above, we are confident in our SIF estimates and believe that there has been a
misunderstanding here.
Concerning spatial variation, Fig. 1 provides a high-level overview of the SIF magnitudes. Further evidence is
presented in Supplementary Figure 1, which explicitly compares the quantity of SIF with the Euclidean
distance to surface drainage visible on optical satellite imagery. Our measurements were concentrated on two
transects, with a spacing that reflects the proximity to surface drainage. Sites FS1, 122, camp, 231, 3u3
constitute one transect. The sites shown in Fig. 1d constitute another transect, which is quasi-tangential to the
main surface channel. We now note these transect configurations in the main text. Concerning a profile
truly tangential to a channel: the location of the channel varies somewhat between years, so this is less feasible
to deploy than it might first appear, and also what a transect equidistant of a stream is one year, would not be
the next. Concerning the measurement stations, these were installed to acquire data in three distinctively
different surface slope regimes and with contrasting surface hydrology in any given melt summer.
Please see also our response to reviewer 1 concerning possible spatial variability in melt.
4. Timing of SIF. There is a section of work on the timing of superimposed ice formation deduced from measurements of the
firn dielectric properties. I found this section very difficult to navigate and not persuasive; the only thing that
seems to be consistent about the probe measurements is how inconsistent they are in time and space. It seems
that very few measurements were actually made and yet apparently firm conclusions are drawn from them.
This is very similar to point 3; it suggests to me that the field experiment was again not up to the task and
in hindsight other measurements would have been made. It’s also not clear to me how important it is to know
the timing of superimposed ice formation – is that really material to this study ? My feeling is this whole is a distraction and could easily be dropped.
On reflection, we agree that knowing the sub-seasonal timing of SIF is not important to our key messages and
is challenging to interpret from our data. We have therefore removed this whole section as suggested.
5. Modelling. The study next leaps into a series of “model” experiments designed to help scale up the field
observations. However, these experiments are tangentially linked to the field measurements at best. The first
“model” is a physical 1D heat transfer model, the second is a linear regression between satellite radar
backscatter and measured superimposed ice formation, and the third is another linear regression between the
modelled superimposed ice formation and cumulative negative degree days derived (I think) from the 1D heat
transfer model. The heat flow model is very loosely related to the field observations as it is contrasted to
temperature profiles that are not directly related to the SIF. Moreover, we can’t really judge how well the
model and observations agree from the data as presented.
We are grateful for these comments, which together with similar comments by reviewer 2 caused us to
fundamentally rethink how we conduct our upscaling. We believe that we have now successfully
addressed this concern and that our response to reviewer 2 answers this major comment.
The satellite radar backscatter is very loosely related to in situ superimposed ice formation; many other factors
affect backscatter and in any case the correlation deduced is largely owing to the clustering of the
measurements into two distinct populations, without which there would be no correlation.
We recognise that in our previous submission there was the potential to conflate radar backscatter with in-situ
SIF, primarily because of the statistical way in which we attempted to conduct our upscaling; however, this
was not our intention. To be clear, we consider backscatter variations in autumn to tell us only about residual
wetness in the near-surface. It is the disappearance of this backscatter that we attribute to SIF, which we now
model physically instead of our previous problematic statistical approach. In the revised manuscript this is
now clearer because we talk only of residual wetness [duration] and not also in terms of sigmaHV0
backscatter strength like previously.
The degree of correlation between satellite derived SIF and negative degree days is relatively weak in any
case, half of the variation is not explained. I find this approach to be quite chaotic, highly empirical, and not
persuasive. I would recommend the authors rethink their approach here entirely and find a better way to add
context and value to their sparse field measurements. The authors do note that regional climate models with
coupled firn process models are another way to study meltwater retention and I agree this would be a better
way to approach this problem.
As explained in our response summary, we have taken heed of these concerns about the upscaling
approach and, we believe, now have a much better methodology with which to deliver our upscaled
calculations.
Concerning the suggestion here that RCMs with coupled firn process models would be a ‘better way’ to
approach the problem: we disagree, and also note that we do not state that they constitute a ‘better way’. As
we have tried to clarify in our re-submission, there are substantial uncertainties/problems remaining with how
RCMs and even observation-based SEB models represent the sub-surface, which makes it desirable to instead
adopt a simplified approach to modelling SIF. Please see in particular the Methods section ‘Modelling
SIF’.
Minor comments
Line 1: I’m not sure the word rivers is helpful here as they are generally associated with land and rain fed. can
you describe in glaciological terminology instead?
The term ‘rivers’ is used elsewhere in the literature. Non exhaustive examples include line 2 of Yang and
Smith (2016, JGR); Smith et al. (2015, PNAS). We have decided to stick with this intuitive terminology rather
than ‘supraglacial streams and rivers’ at every mention.

We have changed to ‘unmeasured’.

known that it will leave the ice sheet locus, or until it has left the ice sheet locus?
Here, in-line with the definition of runoff, water that is assumed to leave the ice sheet locus – updated to
refer to ‘visible runoff’ which is then linked to previous studies in the Introduction.

stated), or that the process of SIF can lead to meltwater being retained
We are a confused by this comment – the text said that ‘SIF….can retain up to roughly three quarters of
locally-produced annual melt’, which doesn’t seem the be converse. Nonetheless, we have tried to clarify in
our revised Abstract.
Line 7: Is the heat flow modelling informed somehow by the field observations? or how else are they linked?
This comment refers to the abstract. We have added a note that the modelling is initialised by in-situ field
observations. The full information is available in the main text as before.
We have added a note that they are used to derive residual wetness.

We prefer not to do this in the abstract, as while the numbers are always a majority (i.e. greater than half),
the
precise value depends on parameter choices. The reader should read the main text for these details.

See previous comment.

Yes, we believe so; see also modified abstract.
